title: A Narrow Window of Opportunity: Diagnosis and Management of Rheumatoid Arthritis in Underserved Populations
description: Earn CME from this on-demand course! For more information, including registration, visit the Arthritis CME website. Overview Rheumatoid arthritis is a chronic autoimmune disorder that is typically characterized by pain and inflammation in the small joints. If untreated, RA may introduce complications that impact the lungs, eyes, bones, and heart. Affecting an estimated 1.3 million US adults,1, 2 RA represents the most common type of autoimmune arthritis.3 Analysis of self-reported National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) data from 2005-2018 indicates a significant difference in RA prevalence among people from different races, educational levels, and poverty-income ratio groups.1 Proactively treating RA will improve the quality of life for patients with the disorder, and many patients who experience symptoms of RA will visit their primary care clinician for treatment. The New Jersey Academy of Family Physicians (NJAFP) assembled a panel of experts to improve patient outcomes by increasing primary care clinicians’ knowledge, comprehension, and performance in managing RA, especially when treating underserved populations. This website reviews current literature and guidelines and provides recommendations for using pharmacologic and non-pharmacologic modalities to develop successful, personalized management plans for patients who report symptoms of RA. Learning Objectives Participants who utilize the education and resources provided on this website will be able to: Recognize signs and symptoms suggestive of RA; Determine when to refer patients with RA to a rheumatologist; Develop a comfort level in prescribing disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs); Help patients understand their disease and engage in shared decision-making; Use motivational interviewing to recognize patients’ concerns; and Recognize and mitigate implicit bias to build a culture of equity in their practice. References Xu Y, Wu Q. Prevalence trend and disparities in rheumatoid arthritis among US adults, 2005-2018. J Clin Med 2021;10:3289. Helmick CG, Felson DT, Lawrence RC, et al. Estimates of the prevalence of arthritis and other rheumatic conditions in the United States. Part I. Arthritis Rheum 2008;58:15-25. American College of Rheumatology. 2021. Rheumatoid Arthritis. https://rheumatology.org/patients/rheumatoid-arthritis

title: Addressing COVID-19 Vaccine Hesitancy: Pregnant Individuals & Other Vulnerable Populations
description: To sign up for this training, visit the New Jersey Hospital Association Training Page . This training is provided by the New Jersey Hospital Association Overview Though much progress has been made since the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic, health care workers must still manage new cases, new variants, and new information. This four-module course will address vaccine hesitancy among vulnerable populations, with an emphasis on pregnant and recently pregnant individuals, and the strategies health care professionals can implement to address these issues. Learner Outcomes At the conclusion of this educational presentation, the participant will be able to: Define key terms related to COVID-19 vaccine (vaccine hesitancy, vaccine confidence, vaccine uptake). Recognize individuals and communities who are at higher risk for COVID-19. Identify possible reasons behind lack of vaccine confidence and lower vaccine uptake among specific high-risk communities (i.e. communities of color, pregnant individuals, individuals planning to become pregnant). Relate factors, including those related to the COVID-19 pandemic, that put individuals at greater risk for anxiety and depression during and after pregnancy. Describe prevention and intervention approaches to help individuals cope with anxiety and depression during and after pregnancy. Review strategies a provider can implement to reach high risk and vulnerable communities to improve vaccine confidence. title: Adult Mental Health First Aid - PUBLIC October 09, 2026
description: Most of us would know how to help if we saw someone having a heart attack—we’d start CPR, or at the very least, call 9-1-1. But too few of us would know how to respond if we saw someone having a panic attack or if we were concerned that a friend or co-worker might be showing signs of alcoholism. Mental Health First Aid is a certification course that takes the fear and hesitation out of starting conversations about mental health and substance use problems by improving understanding and providing an action plan that teaches people to safely and responsibly identify and address a potential mental illness or substance use disorder. Mental Health First Aid for Adults teaches people how to recognize signs of mental health or substance use challenges in adults ages 18 and older, how to offer and provide initial help, and how to guide a person toward appropriate care if necessary. Topics covered include anxiety, depression, psychosis, and addictions. When more people are equipped with the tools they need to start a dialogue, more people can get the help they need. Mental Health First Aiders can even save lives . For more information on this training, contact Jill Ramsey at jdramsey2@alaska.edu

title: AHHA - OB Care in the Emergency Department: How the ED Nurse Can “Deliver”
description: When: On-Demand Self-Paced Where: Online Continuing Education: Available; for more information, visit the event website here. For more information, including registration, visit the event website here. About the Event - Are you an Emergency Department nurse with little or no experience in the Obstetrics Department? - Does the thought of an emergent delivery of a baby in the ED frighten you? - Does your facility not have an Obstetrical Department? - Do you want to learn more about emergent OB conditions that might present in your ED? If you answered yes to any of these questions, this eight-part educational series was designed with you in mind! Throughout this interactive experience, participants engage in simulated learning opportunities, case study discussions, OB and newborn assessments/emergencies, and will review priority interventions for various situations. Content Module 1: Anatomy and physiology in the pregnant person Module 2: Assessment of contractions/fetal heart tones/electronic fetal monitoring Module 3: OB Emergencies – Bleeding Module 4: OB Emergencies – Pre-eclampsia/HELLP syndrome Module 5: OB Emergencies – Prolapsed cord Module 6: OB Emergencies – Shoulder Dystocia Module 7: OB Emergencies – Delivery of Newborn/Newborn Care Module 8: OB Emergencies – Cardia Arrest/Trauma

title: AHHA - Pediatric Assessment and Emergencies
description: When: On-Demand Self Paced Where: Online Continuing Education: Available; see event website for more details. For more information, including registration, visit the event website here . This series will explore assessment and emergency care considerations for the rural pediatric patient. Throughout this interactive experience, participants will be engaged in several learning opportunities, case study discussions/reflections, common pediatric illness/emergencies and reviewing priority interventions for various situations to provide the rural nurse with a solid foundation of core principles and standards of care and practice in caring for the pediatric patient. It is important to recognize that pediatric patients are not little adults. This course is designed to review the anatomy and physiology considerations that differentiate the assessment of pediatric patients from that of caring for the adult patient. Content Module 1: Growth and Development Module 2: Anatomy and physiology. How kids differ from adults Module 3: Respiratory System and Case Studies Module 4: Pediatric Shock Module 5: Childhood Illnesses Module 6: Other Childhood Concerns Module 7: Trauma

title: Alaska Medical Library
description: Visit the Alaska Medical Library here! The Alaska Medical Library (AML) welcomes both students, faculty, staff, and community members to use its services! Trained and professional AML librarians and staff can assist with finding literature and interlibrary loan requests, among many others, see below for more! Housed at the UAA/APU Consortium Library, Second Floor, 3211 Providence Drive, Anchorage, AK 99508 Services for University of Alaska (UAA) and Alaska Pacific University (APU) students, faculty, and staff: Demonstrate UAA/APU Consortium Library resources for academic courses and research projects in nursing, allied health, public health, and medical (WWAMI) programs Work with health sciences faculty to develop instruction sessions and research guides to help students find and use evidence-based resources for their courses Suggest literature search strategies for UAA/APU researchers in nursing, medical, allied health, and public health fields Services for the community: Identify free, reputable consumer health resources for community patrons who contact AML with health-related questions Demonstrate free, reputable consumer health resources for public libraries, school libraries, and other community venues upon request Produce online guides outlining free, reputable consumer health resources Fee-based services for Alaska healthcare professionals and other non-UAA/APU researchers: Search specialty literature for articles and books on a requested topic Deliver journal articles and book chapters to fee-paying AML patrons Provide registered clients with access to databases and ebooks available at AML's website For more information, contact the AML at 907-786-1870, or via email at uaa.aml@alaska.edu Visit the AML Website here , and to register to get access to the extensive evidence based resources, visit the AML Registration website.

title: Alaska Medication for Addiction Treatment Guide 3rd Edition Training Modules
description: When: On-Demand Where: Online Continuing Education: Up to 9 CEs available. Click the button below to register and begin your training! title: Alaska Peer Specialist Training and Support
description: For information on CEUs and to Register, visit the Peer Support Specialist website . What is a Peer Support Professional? Peer Support Professionals are individuals who identify themselves as in recovery: living with a mental illness diagnosis, history of trauma, and/or history of addiction. They may also be a family member of someone who meets that definition. Peer support specialists bring a different perspective when it comes to recovery and helping others through their own journeys. Being able to empathize and empower others at various stages in recovery with personal experiences is what makes Peer Support such an important part of the recovery journey and its success. What do Peer Support Professionals do? - Partner with those they serve and represent them at the table with a treatment team - Assist consumers in understanding the process of services, forms being used, types of questions, and updates - Be present for the consumer - Provide support & encouragement - Assist the consumer in Voice & Choice (teach them self-advocacy) - Offer perspective and hope to the consumer on behalf of the treatment team - Offer insight and perspective to the treatment team on behalf of the consumer - Share personal examples - Support wellness and model recovery values - Support harm reduction as part of the recovery process - Support all stages of recovery and relapse - Offer future oriented dialogue - Be accepting, understanding, non-judgmental, empowering (voice, choice, affirmation, recognition, and advocacy) Training Details We provide weeklong, evening and weekend training options, in-person or via Zoom. Trainings are scheduled throughout the year and throughout the state of Alaska. The training is provided at no cost through support from the Alaska Mental Health Trust Authority and the State of Alaska Division of Behavioral Health. However, you will need to provide your own lunch and transportation. For More Information Contact Jenifer Galvan at Alaska Behavioral Health to see if this opportunity fits into your journey. Phone: 907.444.3666 Email: jgalvan@akbh.org Submit Application for Peer Support Training

title: Alaskan Mobile Crisis Responder:  Essential Skills and Strategies for Challenging Conditions
description: When: On-demand (flexible to meet the needs of the varying and demanding schedules of Crisis Responders) Where: Online and easy to access. Who Should take this Training: This training is designed for helpers in the mental health field who are preparing to enter crisis response work, including crisis teams, mental health clinicians, healthcare providers, and community professionals in rural areas. Continuing Education Credits Available! Overview of Training: The aim of this training is to support crisis responders in focusing their skill sets so they enter this work with confidence, care, and respect . By the end of these modules, crisis responders will be better able to recognize what different mental health crises look like, understand basic techniques and resources for response, gain perspective to make safe and effective decisions, and remain grounded in personal well-being to provide effective care for others in their most vulnerable moments. Learning outcomes include: - Recognizing and responding to a wide range of crises, including mental health, substance use, medical, and behavioral emergencies - Applying rapid assessment tools and triage strategies to determine risk, safety needs, and next steps - Building rapport and using effective communication and de-escalation techniques in high-stress situations - Collaborating across systems (EMS, law enforcement, healthcare, case management) to ensure warm handoffs and coordinated care - Strengthening responder readiness through self-regulation, cultural awareness, and practical field tools Why take this training? You will leave with practical skills, confidence, and strategies to support others in their most vulnerable moments; while protecting your own well-being and strengthening your role in Alaska’s crisis response network. title: An Adventure for Rock Hounds F26
description: Have you ever wondered how the mountains surrounding Homer were formed, or what secrets may lie in the stones and rocks that cover our beaches and trails? Join Taz Tally, aka "The Rock Doc" to find out! Take a journey back through time with Taz down Diamond Creek Trail and along the shoreline, as he reveals the forces of nature that have shaped Kachemak Bay and created one of the great rock-hounding beaches . This two-day course features a short exploration of the rock cycle at Kachemak Bay Campus which includes the use of the college’s classroom rock collections, and a field trip where the students will meet the instructor at the Diamond Creek Trail and see the rock cycle “in action.” Both days are included in the fee but attending the lecture is not necessary for students to fully enjoy the field trip. Students under 14 must be accompanied by a parent. Minors must fill out parent permission paperwork through KBC. Please wear sturdy shoes and bring a walking stick. Other supplies to consider: Rock hammer (or regular hammer) eye protection (goggles or safety glasses) Camera/phone 6" scale Advanced registration and payment are required by the stated deadline. Students may withdraw from community education, non-credit classes/workshops up to three(3) business days prior to the start day of class and receive a 100% refund. After deadlines, no refund is available as instructors have been contracted, materials and supplies purchased, and plans made. KBC reserves the right to cancel this class up to two(2) days before that start date. In the event of cancellation, students will receive a full refund.

title: Assistance with Self-Administered Medications (ASAM) FY27
description: Course Description: Upon completion of this course, staff will acquire the skills and techniques to effectively assist recipients with their medication. This training will meet the Senior and Disability Services Home and Community Based waiver regulations for staff training on Assistance with Self Administration of Medication. It is in compliance with state regulation 7 AAC 130.227 and 7 AAC 125.090 (d)(3). This training does NOT meet requirements for Medication Administration Training, which must be provided by a licensed professional (RN). Learning Objectives: - Describe when staff are responsible to assist clients with their medication needs - Demonstrate a clear understanding of the difference between Medication Administration and Assistance with Self-Administration of Medication - Apply Assistance with the Self-Administration of Medication where needed and appropriate in daily practice. - Appropriately report medication errors. - Properly log and document assisted medications This training is also part of the accredited DSP Training Certification Program with AKTC. Individuals may register and pay directly. We recommend credit card payment for ease and immediate access to training. or Agencies and their employees have 2 options for ASAM registration and payment: We recommend credit card payment for ease and immediate access to training. Check payments require additional steps and a delay in training access. Option 1: Purchase a registration code to issue for use during class registration. Sets of 5, 10, and 20 are available for purchase. To purchase a bulk use registration code, please email chdbusiness@alaska.edu with your agency name and contact person as well as the quantity you would like to purchase. Option 2: Have employee(s) register individually and choose “Employer Pay” during checkout. If "Employer Pay" is chosen during checkout, you must contact Billing at chdbusiness@alaska.edu to set up payment confirmation prior to access being granted in the Blackboard portion of the course. title: CALS 2026 - MD/DO/PA/NP - October 9 - 10 2026
description: Comprehensive Advanced Life Support This course consists of interactive sessions in cardiac, traumatic, pediatric, obstetrical, neonatal and medical advanced life support. Course materials establish the CALS Universal Approach to critically ill or injured patients, which defines the manner by which care providers evaluate and treat emergency patients. The CALS Course was designed to provide physicians, registered nurses, physician assistants, nurse practitioners and paramedics with the opportunity to learn and practice infrequently used lifesaving skills. Participants are encouraged to attend in teams, and courses are limited to 24 participants per session. All applications will be evaluated for admission to the course. Priority will be given to rural providers. Skills Taught Include: - The CALS Universal Approach - Trauma Patient Assessment - Video laryngoscopy - Cricothyrotomy - Needle thoracostomy - Chest tube insertion - Percutaneous pericardiocentesis - Vascular Access (IO and Ultrasound Assisted) - Emergency Deliveries - Umbilical Catheterization - Pelvic Wrap - Helmet removal - Traction splint - Bleeding Control including wound packing and tourniquet application - FAST Exam CALS Course Objectives: - Demonstrate the ability to problem solve in a variety of clinical situations. Identify key threats and demonstrate therapeutic interventions. - Discuss the roles of each team member involved in patient evaluation and treatment. - Perform skills consistent with the provider’s role on the advanced life support team. For eligibility and content questions, contact akcalsprogram@gmail.com . You will receive automated emails from info@calsprogram.org and notifications@learnupon.com regarding your registration and course materials. We highly encourage adding these two email addresses to your email contacts to avoid important messages being sent to spam. Course materials will be available within 60 days of the course start date. This is a blended learning course, so you will have 6-8 hours of eLearning modules to complete on your own before the in-person course. title: CALS 2026 - RN/Paramedic - October 9 - 10 2026
description: Comprehensive Advanced Life Support This course consists of interactive sessions in cardiac, traumatic, pediatric, obstetrical, neonatal and medical advanced life support. Course materials establish the CALS Universal Approach to critically ill or injured patients, which defines the manner by which care providers evaluate and treat emergency patients. The CALS Course was designed to provide physicians, registered nurses, physician assistants, nurse practitioners and paramedics with the opportunity to learn and practice infrequently used lifesaving skills. Participants are encouraged to attend in teams, and courses are limited to 24 participants per session. All applications will be evaluated for admission to the course. Priority will be given to rural providers. Skills Taught Include: - The CALS Universal Approach - Trauma Patient Assessment - Video laryngoscopy - Cricothyrotomy - Needle thoracostomy - Chest tube insertion - Percutaneous pericardiocentesis - Vascular Access (IO and Ultrasound Assisted) - Emergency Deliveries - Umbilical Catheterization - Pelvic Wrap - Helmet removal - Traction splint - Bleeding Control including wound packing and tourniquet application - FAST Exam CALS Course Objectives: - Demonstrate the ability to problem solve in a variety of clinical situations. Identify key threats and demonstrate therapeutic interventions. - Discuss the roles of each team member involved in patient evaluation and treatment. - Perform skills consistent with the provider’s role on the advanced life support team. For eligibility and content questions, contact akcalsprogram@gmail.com . You will receive automated emails from info@calsprogram.org and notifications@learnupon.com regarding your registration and course materials. We highly encourage adding these two email addresses to your email contacts to avoid important messages being sent to spam. Course materials will be available within 60 days of the course start date. This is a blended learning course, so you will have 6-8 hours of eLearning modules to complete on your own before the in-person course. Hub and spoke knowledge-sharing networks create a learning loop: Community participants learn from specialists Community participants learn from each other Specialists learn from community participants as best practices emerge ECHO (Extension for Community Healthcare Outcomes) uses videoconferencing technology to connect a team of interdisciplinary experts with primary care providers, other health services professionals, and community members. title: Community Relationship Building and Key Concepts of Support for DSPs (PRIVATE) August 27, 2026
description: This training is intended to focus, guide, and change our philosophy on how we work with people, thus changing the way we work with people. Whether working with a person you support, a family member you care for, a peer or just someone you need to change your approach with, these concepts encompass a recipe for walking alongside a person, not just to meet goals and objectives but to grow and learn and develop hobbies and interests and relationships and connections, resulting in a full and meaningful life. This training is a total of 12 hours, separated into six (2-hour) sessions taught once a week for six weeks. The training includes “homework” and directly working with a person with a disability to support and focus on enhancement of natural supports during the six weeks of the training. Class 1 – How to Develop Partnerships - Objective : Learn how to provide support to people we serve to direct their own lives through healthy relationships with peers, supervisors and families. Class 2 - How to Provide Options, Consider Risks and Become 'Part of' - Objective 1: Learn how to support a person to try new things and understand choices have risks so they can make an informed choice. - Objective 2: Learn how to support integration and inclusion in the community for those we support. Class 3 - How We Seek Information and Show We are 'Present' - Objective 1: Learn to identify and use resources that promote growth, change and autonomy in how we support people we serve. - Objective 2: Learn active listening skills by being focused and attentive. Class 4 - How to Build Bridges, not Barriers - Objective : Learn how to help people we support to pursue new experiences and explore assistive technology and other options that increase their access to their community. Class 5 - How to Make Contributions and Honor Commitments - Objective 1: Learn how to provide support to the people we serve to follow through and honor their chosen commitments. - Objective 2: Learn how to provide support to people we serve to engage in their community through volunteering, giving back and experiencing community engagement. Class 6 - Embrace the role of Teacher, Mentor, and Coach - Objective : Learn how to apply supportive teaching with someone you serve. title: Cultural Connections Guide and Educator Training
description: When: On-Demand Where: Online For more information, including registration to the class, visit the link here. An interactive training for Alaska guides and educators. This course explores Alaska Native cultures and how to respectfully share information with summer visitors. Modules - Diversity of Alaska Native People - Resilience of Alaska Native Cultures - Cultural Celebrations - Sharing Respectfully Learning Outcomes - Students will be able to identify and demonstrate communication methods that privilege Alaska Native perspectives; - Students will be able to articulate a high level perspective of the legal landscape for Alaska Natives; - Students will be able to describe some of the key aspects of Alaska Native culture; - Students will be able to clearly explain why Alaska Native cultures matter; - Students will be able to articulate how they choose what they share about Alaska Native cultures while guiding.

description: When: On-Demand Where: Online Continuing Education: This activity was planned by and for the healthcare team, and learners will receive up to 10.5 Interprofessional Continuing Education (IPCE) credit for learning and change. For more information about interprofessional Continuing Education, visit the Joint Accreditation website here. Welcome to the Cultural Foundations for Healthcare Providers in Alaska training! Develop increased awareness and knowledge around culturally sustaining healthcare practices that foster respectful and reciprocal relationships with patients and colleagues in Alaskan rural communities. Learn about the different regions in Alaska, the health hubs in each, and the history of the people. This self-paced training is meant to be completed over several days.

title: Cultural Humility in Behavioral Health Care
description: When & Where: Online, self-paced, approximately 2 hours For more information, and to register for this event, visit UW Medicine's registration website here. What You’ll Learn: Participants will enhance their ability to provide culturally responsive care by understanding and applying the principles of cultural humility. Key topics include: - Behavioral health equity and its role in care delivery - The distinction between cultural humility and cultural competence - The impact of implicit and explicit bias on professional practice - Practical strategies for fostering inclusivity and sensitivity in behavioral health settings - Through interactive scenarios and self-reflection exercises, participants will build skills that promote more compassionate, equitable, and effective care, contributing to a more inclusive behavioral health care environment. 2 CE's available! Each module offers approximately one hour of focused learning and you will receive a continuing education certificate for each module you complete. You have the autonomy to progress at your own pace, pausing and resuming as needed.

title: Dementia Care Skills September 25, 2026
description: This workshop introduces participants to dementia; how it affects the brain, sensory system and visual range. Participants will discuss normal vs not normal aging traits. Participants will learn & practice Positive Physical Approach® interaction skills to navigate challenging behaviors and role play common caregiving situations utilizing their physical skills, including ways to ‘activate’ their care partner. Objectives: 1. Discuss how dementia changes the brain and how those changes affect the person living with dementia. 2. Learn about Normal aging traits vs Not Normal aging traits. 3. Learn how to describe the 5 sensory input processing systems and the impact dementia has on those systems 4. Participants will learn 3 PAC skills: Positive Physical Approach®, Hand Under Hand®, Positive Action Starters® 5. Learners will practice using Positive Approach to Care skills through roll-playing scenarios.

title: ED A555B: Multicultural Studies for Alaska's Teachers
description: Provides a framework for understanding multicultural education in the context of the classroom, community, and society. Focuses on ways to build relationships within classrooms that support multicultural learning. Presents an overview of Alaska Native cultures, historical events, and worldviews. Explores contemporary education issues, including planning and implementation of classroom activities and strategies that fosters growth in teachers to accept and appreciate all cultures and value the rich diversity of the students in their classrooms and beyond. Incorporates Alaska Standards for Culturally Responsive Schools and the Guidelines for Preparing Culturally Responsive teachers. This course satisfies the State of Alaska multicultural education/cross-cultural communication requirement for initial teacher certification of AS 14.20.020(h) and 4 AAC 12.075(b).

title: ED A555K: Culturally Responsive Teaching: A Framework for Teaching and Learning in Alaska
description: Examines culturally responsive teaching as a model for teaching and learning in Alaska. Provides educators with opportunities to examine and analyze current research, theory, principles, and effective instructional practices in curriculum and instruction. Focuses on current content theory, research, and knowledge; standards-based instructional design and practice; assessment and evaluation practices; and integrated/interdisciplinary curriculum design. Promotes application of effective curriculum development and instruction that utilizes collaboration as well as individual reflection. This course satisfies the State of Alaska multicultural education/cross-cultural communication requirement for initial teacher certification of AS 14.20.020(h) and 4 AAC 12.075(b).

title: Ethics and Boundaries for the Direct Care Worker FY27
description: Designed for the residential direct service provider, this training addresses professional ethical behavior relative to conflicts of interest, personal and client property, solving ethical dilemmas, and recognizing issues of ethics and boundaries in the workplace. Ethics are the guiding principles for Direct Support Professionals (DSPs) in service delivery. Delivering high quality services while maintaining professional boundaries is essential to providing excellent support, maintaining healthy relationships, and protecting your own well-being and that of your clients. Person Centered Thinking guides every decision as DSPs support individuals to live the life they choose. All of the roles that a DSP fills maintains a common focus on supporting individuals to live the life they desire. DSPs are the teacher, partner, resource, ambassador, advocate, encourager and provider. DSPs are not a boss or parent and the job carries a great deal of responsibility to understand and clearly fulfill these roles. Unlike a parent, legal guardian, or conservator, DSPs do not have the responsibility to make important life decisions for the individuals they work for and with (such as medical or financial decisions). Instead, the individuals themselves, with the assistance of parents, legal guardians, or conservators, as appropriate, make decisions about their own lives and the DSP supports and assists individuals in their everyday life. Person Centered Thinking guides every decision as DSPs support individuals to live the life they choose. Learning Objectives: - Understand the role of the DSP, including the multiple hats worn in this position - Understand how to navigate ethical dilemmas - Learn how best to support you client while maintaining professional boundaries This training is also part of the accredited DSP Training Certification Program with AKTC.

description: When: Aug 26-29, 2026 | 9:00 am-5:00 pm Where: UAA, Anchorage, AK (Change from previous venue, also in Anchorage) Host: The Mental Health Co-Op in support of Alaska EFT CE Credits: 28 credits. NBCC credits through The Mental Health Co-Op - The Mental Health Co-Op has been approved by NBCC as an Approved Continuing Education Provider, ACEP No. 7982. Programs that do not qualify for NBCC credit are clearly identified. The Mental Health Co-Op is solely responsible for all aspects of the programs. For more information, including registration, visit the event website here. Overview: In this workshop participants will learn concepts and gain skills for the application of therapeutic techniques that support treatment of depression, anxiety, and trauma disorders, as well as resolution of interpersonal and intrapersonal conflict. An Externship in Emotionally Focused Couples Therapy® (EFCT) is an immersive four-day training experience foundational for therapists aiming to specialize in EFCT. Led by certified trainers, it offers a comprehensive introduction to the EFCT model, focusing on the science of attachment and the systematic approach to couple therapy. This training is crucial for therapists because it equips them with the necessary skills to foster secure, resilient relationships in therapy. It’s the first step in formal EFCT training, opening the door to advanced practice and certification and enhancing therapists’ efficacy and confidence in their clinical work with couples. *** Tools and concepts can be applied to individual, couple, and family work. Objectives for the Externship: - Participants will obtain a clear understanding of the basic experiential and systemic concepts of an “Emotionally Focused” approach to therapy. - Participants will be able to assess and diagram clients in the web of their interpersonal attachments and conceptualize relationship distress and repair based on theories of attachment and emotion. - Participants will develop skills in sharing and maintaining an engaged, open, and collaborative alliance with clients. - Participants will develop skills in the five moves of the basic macro-intervention – the EFT Tango –to change patterns of affect regulation, models of self and others, strategies for engaging others, and interactional patterns. - Participants will develop skills in EFT micro-interventions taken from experiential and attachment systemic models of intervention. - Participants will develop skills in overcoming common blocks and impasses in couple therapy, shaping core corrective emotional experiences that lead to constructive dependency and what Rogers termed ‘existential living.’ Investment: $575 - $1,150. title: Fall Prevention for Direct Care Workers FY27
description: Falls are a common and serious health threat to individuals with disabilities including adults 65 and older. Every year more than 1 in 4 older adults falls, but more than half of those who fall don’t tell their healthcare provider leading to high healthcare costs and hospitalization. This training and the resources shared will help direct service providers self-assess the environment of the assisted living home (ALH) or recipient's environment to put fall prevention strategies into practice. This training is offered exclusively online, on-demand and self-guided. If interested in more information about this training, please contact Liz Gerken-Miller, egerken@alaska.edu Learning Objectives: - Learn to assess for environmental hazards that can increase risk for falls - Understand best practices in fall prevention strategies for DSPs This training is also part of the accredited DSP Training Certification Program with AKTC.

title: Foundation of Peer Support Professionals
description: When: On-demand Where: Online Continuing Education: 1 Contact Hour Click the Register button below to add the course to your cart, and check out in the upper right! Welcome to the School of Social Work - Foundations of Peer Support Professionals ! Peer support is rooted in the simple yet powerful idea that people who have experienced and overcome life challenges can offer a unique form of help to others facing similar struggles. What began as informal, person-to-person encouragement has evolved into a recognized and valued professional role across recovery-oriented systems of care. This training will provide a foundation in the history, principles, and research behind peer support, explore the critical role of lived experience. By understanding the values and evidence that guide this work, attendees will be better equipped to support peer support specialist roles and services.

title: Fundamentals of Arctic Engineering - Fall 2026
description: This course introduces students to a broad spectrum of engineering challenges that are unique to cold regions of the world. Physical principles and practical data collection, analysis, design, and construction methods are discussed. Students gain a working knowledge of cold regions engineering problems and modern solutions as a basis for more detailed study. Information in the format of narrated slide presentations, videos, and other online study aids is presented in 10 daily increments. Students should budget 4 to 5 hours per day for reviewing online materials, participating in discussions, and accomplishing daily exercises. Students may choose their own optimum learning times to maintain the daily pace. The tenth day of the course includes a comprehensive final examination. Licensing Approval : The UAA "Fundamentals of Arctic Engineering" course is approved by the Alaska State Board of Registration for Architects, Engineers, and Land Surveyors to satisfy the Alaska regulation governing registration and licensing (12 AAC 36.110), which reads "...An applicant for registration as an architect, engineer, or landscape architect must have successfully completed a board-approved university level course in arctic engineering or its equivalent...." The Board's Licensing Examiner, with permission of each student, will be notified by the UAA College of Engineering of the names of those students who pass the course. Instructive online presentations and materials will provide students with an introductory working knowledge of Arctic design principles, as they relate to the major design areas of architecture, engineering, land surveying, and landscape architecture, including information about: C old regions natural conditions and engineering challenges, A ssociated specialized language and units of measure, L ocation, interpretation, and application of public information about cold regions physical conditions, Application of fundamental physical principles to solve common cold regions engineering problems, and Introduction to more sophisticated and complex solutions. If you choose to pay with a check, please send to UAA Office of the Bursar, PO Box 141609, Anchorage, AK 99514. Memo should state: ES AC030, CoEng ACWE account .

description: When: On-Demand Where: Online For more information, including registration, visit the GERO Nurse Prep website here. Gero Nurse Prep is an online training course designed to prepare RNs who care for elders to attain board certification in Gerontological Nursing by the American Nurses Credentialing Center (ANCC) . This course equips RNs with a broad array of clinical knowledge, skills and competencies that are tested on the ANCC certification exam and essential for quality gerontological nursing practice and leadership of elder care teams. Content in the course is mapped to ANCC test outline to ensure success in ANCC certification in Gerontological Nursing. - Gero Nurse Prep Alums have a 96% pass rate on the certification exam. - 30 ANCC contact hours by the UNMC CON CiPDI , a Jointly Accredited Provider. - 10 online educational modules, complete with content, assigned readings, learning activities, & numerous resources. - Practice test opportunities including a simulated certification exam & test taking strategies & tips. - End of course forum with tips from Gero Nurse Prep Alums who passed the certification exam - User friendly format available 24/7 on any computer with Internet access. title: Grief Literacy for School Social Workers: Supporting  Students Experiencing Grief and Loss
description: When: On-Demand Where: Online Continuing Education: Pending for Social Work credit. To register, click the "Register" button below to add to your cart, and then check out. The purpose of this course is to increase the grief literacy of school social workers in Alaska and to support school social workers in providing leadership to create school communities that are responsive and supportive during a time of loss. Schools are an important place for children to receive support when they have experienced a loss, because schools are familiar, students spend a lot of time at school, and schools employ many professionals who can support grieving students (Schonfled & Quackenbush, 2021). This training is appropriate for social workers working in educational settings that include early intervention (birth to three) and K-12 education. The objectives of this training are to: - Develop basic grief literacy knowledge and skills by exploring common myths about childhood grief and loss and defining key terms related to grief and loss. - Understand the impact of childhood grief and loss on students. - Explore the roles, knowledge, and skills of the school social worker in supporting students with grief and loss. This training is part of the Advancing School Social Work in Alaska initiative and is funded by a grant (P116Z240135) from the U.S. Department of Education

title: Healthcare Provider Burnout: Prevalence, Consequences, and Solutions with Dr. Kari Bernard
description: When: On-Demand Where: Online via Blackboard Continuing Education: This activity was planned by and for the healthcare team, and learners will receive up to 5 Interprofessional Continuing Education (IPCE) credit for learning and change. For more information about interprofessional Continuing Education, visit the Joint Accreditation website here. Welcome to the Healthcare Provider Burnout: Prevalence, Consequences, and Solutions program. As you complete the 5 on-demand modules at your own pace, you will earn CME credit while exploring how large proportions of historically resilient professionals are becoming exhausted and cynical trying to deliver patient care. The modules outline system-level causes of burnout, its consequences, which extend well beyond the providers, and what can be done to treat and prevent burnout. Didactic modules are interspersed with interactive exercises that allow you to apply the material to your current circumstances. It is recommended that you complete the program over 5 weeks. This will allow you to work through each module one week at a time.

title: Hearing Distressing Voices October 27, 2026
description: The Hearing Distressing Voices (HDV) workshop is a groundbreaking and empathy-building experience that helps participants understand the challenges and strengths of people who experience psychosis. The workshop is a 4-hour experiential training that provides a simulated experience of what it may be like to hear voices that are distressing. Participants use MP3 players and ear buds to simulate hearing distressing voices while participating in scenarios and environments in which to navigate. This workshop is intended for non-voice hearers. A group discussion of the experience follows along with helpful information from voice hearers regarding coping and support. Agencies can receive FREE seats in the training for their staff in exchange for volunteering staff and resources for the workshop. Please contact Jill Ramsey at jdramsey@alaska.edu or call 907-264-6228 for more information. Learning Objectives: • Increase knowledge about voice-hearing experiences. • Experience more empathy for and understanding of those hearing distressing voices. • Gain more confidence in interactions with people experiencing distressing voices. • Learn ways to effectively communicate with people who hear voices. • Learn effective ways to support individuals to cope with distress related to hearing voices. NOTE: There are two separate trainings one in the AM and one in the PM. Double check which training you are registering for.

title: Improvisation Theater - Fall 2026
description: This is a fun-loving, confidence building class that explores the use of role play to explore creativity and build a sense of community. Students will experience team building activities using the drama skills of creating tableau, pantomimed action, use of representative props and costumes to bring original and simple scripts to life. Students will experiment with the use of voice, body, imagination, and cooperative team work to explore playwriting. Elements of Playback Theatre will be introduced. This is a form of theatre that combines real-life storytelling with improvised dramatization. Class will meet once per week for eight weeks. Each session is two hours.

title: NC AHEC Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion (DEI) Modules for Primary Care Clinical and Non-Clinical Staff
description: NC AHEC Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion (DEI) Modules for Primary Care Clinical and Non-clinical Staff Modules are available on demand. CEU Credits are available! For more information, visit the North Carolina AHEC DEI module website . Healthcare providers are required to be competent not only in medicine but also in communication and caring for people with different disease burdens, socio-cultural realities, expectations, values, and beliefs. Be it the result of a language barrier, differences in philosophy, differences in cultural norms (and expectations), or even cultural bias, lack of diversity can lead to communication breakdown with patients. Consequently, when patients cannot fully communicate or express their needs, health inequities and health disparities occur. Health equity means ensuring that every person in every community can get the same high-quality care regardless of individual characteristics, such as ethnicity, gender or geographic location. A number of social, economic and cultural factors significantly affect both physical and mental health. Healthcare providers require education to recognize and eliminate these disadvantages that lead to healthcare disparities through initiatives that increase diversity in leadership, improve training for cultural humility, and strengthen community partnerships. The program will consist of 12 individual modules and will focus on implementing DEI strategies that are proven to improve patient care including: • Articulating how DEI plays a heightened and essential role in today’s healthcare environment • Educating clinical providers and non-clinical staff on fundamental concepts, such as cultural humility, structural racism, and other relevant content to assist providers and staff to increase knowledge and adopt equitable practices • Integrating DEI values and core principles into the patient care environment • Building core competency and shared language across staff

title: One Health Epidemiology
description: The Arctic is warming three to four times faster than the rest of the planet, and rural communities in Alaska rely on and live closely with animals. This makes our communities particularly vulnerable to climate change impacts, including emerging infectious diseases in both animal and human populations. In today's landscape, clinicians able to apply a One Health framework—the understanding that the health of humans, animals, and ecosystems are interconnected—will be better prepared to meet the challenges ahead. Whether you're a veterinarian managing a reindeer herd or a nurse practitioner caring for individual patients, the principles needed to test for, analyze, and respond to emerging threats are transferable across disciplines. One Health Epidemiology introduces the foundational principles and methods used to study the distribution and determinants of disease in human and animal populations. Through real-world examples, students learn to analyze data, assess risk, evaluate study designs and preventive health interventions, and monitor emerging health threats. Emphasis is placed on climate change impacts in the Arctic and how epidemiology can guide community-level action to improve outcomes for humans, animals, and the environment. TARGET AUDIENCE This online asynchronous self-paced course is open to anyone—no university enrollment required. Nurses, NPs, Physicians, PAs, and other licensed healthcare professionals can take this evidence-based course to earn 14 Jointly Accredited Interprofessional Continuing Education credits, but anyone can take the course. If you don't need CME/CEUs, you can still earn a certificate of completion to demonstrate your learning. All are welcome! LEARNING OBJECTIVES Upon completion of the course, students will be able to: - Critique epidemiologic studies and apply to clinical or public health practice. - Analyze population health research and data to guide clinical or community health decision-making. - Assess causality and risk in clinical situations. - Analyze screening, testing, and interpretation in clinical practice. - Use epidemiologic methods to improve health outcomes for people, animals, or ecosystems. FORMAT & EVALUATION OF LEARNING Online asynchronous course delivered via Blackboard. Knowledge checks throughout the course and video-guided practice problems supplement learning from lectures and readings. Learners are assessed with four timed tests, each with 20 questions. Two attempts are allowed per test. An average of ≥70% on the four graded assessments is a passing grade. description: To register for this training, visit the PriMed Website here . The nation is facing competing public health issues: the need to treat a large number of Americans with acute and chronic pain versus the crisis of prescription opioid abuse. NAO has partnered with Pri -Med’s P.A.C.T. Practical Approaches to Comprehensive Treatment of Pain curriculum to provide education to AHEC’s engaged in prescribing and or treating patients with opioid analgesics. This program is intended for those involved with direct patient care, including all members of the healthcare team. P.A.C.T. Practical Approaches to Comprehensive Treatment of Pain curriculum focuses on improving clinicians’ ability to recognize, diagnose, and classify pain; educating clinicians on the full spectrum of pain management options, including non-opioid pharmacologic interventions; and providing risk reduction strategies through integration of opioids into individualized pain management plans. Presenting clinicians with a thorough review of the FDA’s “ Opioid Analgesic REMS Education Blueprint for Health Care Providers Involved in the Treatment and Monitoring of Patients with Pain ” will allow clinicians to provide evidence-based pain management to their patients on a daily basis. This curriculum will also provide tools to help clinicians mitigate issues associated with opioid therapies, recognizing the signs and symptoms of opioid dependence and abuse to best manage patients’ pain and medication use, and take steps to avert the opioid addiction crisis. This activity is supported by an independent educational grant from the Opioid Analgesic REMS Program Companies. Please see https://ce.opioidanalgesicrems.com/RpcCEUI/rems/pdf/resources/List_of_RPC_Companies.pdf for a listing of REMS Program Companies. title: Presentation and Management of Pediatric Acute-Onset Neuropsychiatric Syndrome (PANS)
description: CACHE · Continuing Education Health & Behavioral Health · On-Demand · Online · Free ▶ Access the Video View Full CACHE Training Catalog → ✓ Continuing Education credits may be available — see provider site. Overview Internet Enduring Material sponsored by Stanford University School of Medicine · Departments of Pediatrics, Psychiatry & Behavioral Health. This CME activity provides a practical approach to recognizing and managing Pediatric Acute-Onset Neuropsychiatric Syndrome (PANS). PANS is relatively newly understood, under-identified, and under-treated in clinical practice. Infectious and inflammatory diseases can present with severe, debilitating psychiatric and neurological symptoms — and when those connections go unrecognized, clinical treatment may be missed or delayed. The course covers case scenarios, physical exam techniques for neurological soft signs, treatment algorithms, family education, multidisciplinary coordination, and school accommodations. What You'll Learn ✓ Recognize early PANS symptoms and presentation patterns ✓ Understand the connection between infection, inflammation, and neuropsychiatric symptoms ✓ Perform physical examination for neurological soft signs ✓ Apply evidence-based treatment algorithms ✓ Coordinate multidisciplinary care across clinical settings ✓ Support family education and school accommodation planning Intended Audience Primary Care Family Practice Pediatrics Neurology Psychiatry Emergency Medicine Adolescent Medicine Otolaryngology Allergy / Immunology Rheumatology Urology Sleep Medicine Provider Northwest PANDAS/PANS Network 501c3 · Pacific Northwest · PANS / PANDAS / AE — raising awareness, providing education, advocating for legislative change, and supporting local research. title: The Menopause Transition: Optimally Protecting Emotional Health
description: Overview Menopause is a universal milestone in the life cycle of women and every woman’s experience of this phase of life is unique and influenced by a variety of factors. The transition from normal ovarian function to the near-complete loss of estrogen production comes with a range of psychological, endocrinological, and physical changes which occur over years. Though some women go through the menopausal transition asymptomatic or with few symptoms, over 85% experience the effects of estrogen fluctuation and eventual deficiency – sweating, hot flashes, insomnia, discomfort, and vaginal dryness. These symptoms can range from mild to moderate discomfort to symptoms that are severe and disabling and are all influenced by psychological, ethnic, and socio-cultural factors. Learning Objectives Participants who utilize the enduring education provided on this website will be able to: Recognize that in the clinical setting, women from different ethnic backgrounds will characterize menopause and its associated symptoms differently. Employ patient-focused, culturally relevant communication techniques when counseling patients regarding menopause and their menopausal symptoms. Utilize a patient-centered, shared-decision making approach in the evaluation and management of menopausal symptoms, including depression. Provide objective, up-to-date, evidence-based education regarding possible menopausal symptom treatment options along with an individualized management and follow-up plan This course is worth CME! For more information, including registration and CME, visit the New Jersey Academy of Family Physicians website.

description: Trust-Based Relational Intervention (TBRI®) is an evidence-based attachment-based, trauma-informed, whole-child approach to meeting the needs of children and youth who have experienced early adversity, toxic stress, and/or relational trauma. TBRI® has been used throughout the world to heal children who “come from hard places”.
